newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: UK's Major, majority gone, lectures EU on jobs.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major, majority gone, lectures EU on jobs.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, defiant despite losing his parliamentary majority, on Friday lectured European leaders on jobs.

As his colleagues wrangled over how to stop members of a European single currency overspending and how to reform the bloc's institutions, Major took them to task, saying their employment policies were far too rigid.
British officials said Major, who played down the summit on Friday as one where no "serious decisions are going to be taken", told the other leaders they should copy Britain.
Major reinforced his message by handing out a document with charts designed to prove his case that reforms of trade union law and deregulation have revolutionised Britain's jobs market.
But he hardly provoked a ripple at the Dublin summit, where his shaky grasp on power and the imminent prospect of a more Europe-friendly Labour government has undermined his authority.
"Nobody reacted," said one minister at the meeting who asked not to be named. "It was a monologue. There was no dialogue."
Major's jobs lecture was seen by Britain's media as aimed as much at British voters as at his fellow leaders.
With an election looming any time before May, Major is desperate to boost his party's standing by showing the Conservatives as the party of jobs and low taxes.
But the so-called "feelgood" factor is proving elusive and Europe is again provoking civil war in his increasingly skittish and divided Conservative party, now staring defeat in the face.

Polls show him 20 points or more behind Labour and Major was delivered another body blow on Thursday with a crushing by-election victory for the opposition Labour party in the former mining area of Barnsley in northern England.
The vote means the Conservatives are now level pegging with the opposition parties in parliament.

But Major, who has pledged to hang on to office, shrugged off the defeat, telling reporters, "I don't think it is going to make a material difference...Provided people behave themselves, we will get through to our preferred (election) date."

But he showed his underlying bitterness in an attack on Labour leader Tony Blair, who has been in Dublin for a pre-summit meeting of European socialist leaders, and in a warning to fellow heads of government not to write him off yet.

"There is no doubt that some of the socialist countries would prefer to deal with a socialist government in the United Kingdom...The socialists across Europe, including Mr Blair, meet routinely before summits and try to concert their positions.
"Well I don't think that the British people would like their national decisions taken behind closed doors in meetings of socialist leaders. So I am here, they will have to deal with me.
"And I expect to be here after the election and they will have to deal with me," Major told reporters.
